title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 812–814 (Night 171, continuing nights-170), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 171 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān, grieved by his son's refusal to marry but too fond of him to press it, waits a full year while the boy grows ever more beautiful, praised in rhymed prose and verse. Then he asks again, and Qamar al-Zamān, though he owns that God has commanded obedience to a father, refuses once more: he has read in the books of the ancients and the moderns of women's guile, and he quotes two poems against them. The king, too loving to answer him, breaks up the audience and takes counsel with his vizier, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-first night,
sentences.n: Last night needed the special formula for a round number (al-mūfiya li-al-sabʿīn); with a unit in front the plain pattern returns: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, feminine to agree with layla, then wa-al-sabʿūn, “and the seventy”, in its cardinal form, then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”. The alif of المائة is silent: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ لَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنْ وَلَدِهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهِ ظَلَامًا وَاغْتَمَّ عَلَي عَدَمِ مُطَاوَعَةِ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ لَهُ فِيمَا أَشَارَ عَلَيْهِ بِهِ مِنْ أَمْرِ الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna lammā samiʿa min waladihi hādhā al-kalāma ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihi ẓalāman wa-ightamma ʿalā ʿadami muṭāwaʿati waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni lahu fīmā ashāra ʿalayhi bihi min amri al-zawāji
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān, when he-heard from his-son this speech, the light in his-face became darkness, and he-grieved over the lack of complying of his-son Qamar al-Zamān with-him in-what he-had-counselled him with-it, of the matter of the marriage.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when King Shahramān heard these words from his son, the light in his face turned to darkness, and he was grieved that his son Qamar al-Zamān would not yield to him in the matter of marriage that he had pressed upon him.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the story by repeating, almost word for word, the last sentence of the night before. The sentence starts with the king as the subject of anna, is interrupted by the lammā clause, and then carries on with a new subject (ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu, “the light became”): a loose but normal narrative build. ightamma, Form VIII, “to be grieved”, here with ʿalā, “over”; the print writes ʿalā as علي, with ي for ى, a habit of the edition. ʿadam, “absence, lack”, before a verbal noun is the usual way to say “not doing”: ʿadam muṭāwaʿa, “the not-complying”; muṭāwaʿa is the verbal noun of ṭāwaʿa (III), “to comply with”, and the person complied with takes la-: lahu, “with him”. ashāra ʿalā … bi-, Form IV, “to advise someone (ʿalā) to do something (bi-)”: ʿalayhi is the son, the -hi of bihi points back to mā, “what he advised him”, and min amr al-zawāj spells out what that was. The shadda of اغتمّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ شِدَّةِ مَحَبَّتِهِ لَهُ لَمْ يَرْضَ أَنْ يُكَرِّرَ عَلَيْهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَلَمْ يُغْضِبْهُ بَلْ أَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَأَكْرَمَهُ وَلَاطَفَهُ بِكُلِّ مَا يَجْلِبُ الْمَحَبَّةَ إِلَى الْقَلْبِ
sentences.tr: wa-min shiddati maḥabbatihi lahu lam yarḍa an yukarrira ʿalayhi hādhā al-kalāma wa-lam yughḍibhu bal aqbala ʿalayhi wa-akramahu wa-lāṭafahu bi-kulli mā yajlibu al-maḥabbata ilā al-qalbi
sentences.l: And from the intensity of his-love for-him, he-did-not-consent to repeat upon-him this speech, and he-did-not anger-him; rather he-turned toward-him and honoured-him and was-gentle-with-him with every-thing that draws the love to the heart.
sentences.i: So great was his love for him that he would not press the matter on him again, nor provoke him; instead he turned to him warmly, honoured him, and showed him every kindness that wins a heart's affection.
sentences.n: min shiddati …, “out of the intensity of …”, gives the cause. lam yarḍa: jussive of raḍiya, yarḍā, “to be content, consent”; after lam the final long vowel drops. an yukarrira, Form II subjunctive, “to repeat”, with ʿalā of the person addressed. lam yughḍibhu, Form IV jussive, “to anger”, + -hu, “him”. bal, “rather, on the contrary”. aqbala ʿalā, Form IV, “to turn towards someone, give him one's attention”: the verb chooses ʿalā. lāṭafa, Form III, “to treat gently, be kind to”. bi-kulli mā, “with everything that”: bi- names the means. The shadda of محبّته is printed.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذَلِكَ وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ يَزْدَادُ حُسْنًا وَجَمَالًا وَظَرْفًا وَدَلَالًا
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni kulla yawmin yazdādu ḥusnan wa-jamālan wa-ẓarfan wa-dalālan
sentences.l: All that, and Qamar al-Zamān every day increases (in) beauty and loveliness and grace and coquetry.
sentences.i: And all this while Qamar al-Zamān grew daily in beauty and loveliness, in charm and in winning ways.
sentences.n: kullu dhālika wa-…, “all that, with …”, i.e. “all this time, while …”: a narrative idiom in which wa- introduces a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. The case of kull is not printed; it is pointed here as a loose nominative, but kulla, adverbial, “throughout all that”, is equally possible. kulla yawmin, adverbial accusative, “every day”. yazdādu, Form VIII of zāda, “to grow, increase”, takes what is gained in the accusative of specification: ḥusnan, “in beauty”. The imperfect describes what was going on at the time. dalāl is the playful, self-assured airs of the beloved, a virtue in love poetry. The rhyme falls on jamālan / dalālan.

sentences.t: فَصَبَرَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ عَلَي وَلَدِهِ سَنَةً كَامِلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-ṣabara al-maliku Shahramānu ʿalā waladihi sanatan kāmilatan
sentences.l: So King Shahramān was-patient with his-son a-year complete.
sentences.i: So King Shahramān bore with his son for a whole year.
sentences.n: ṣabara ʿalā, “to be patient with, bear with”: the verb chooses ʿalā, printed علي again. sanatan kāmilatan, accusative of duration, “for a full year”.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهُ قَدْ كَمُلَ بِالْفَصَاحَةِ وَالْمَلَاحَةِ وَتَهَتَّكَتْ فِي حُسْنِهِ الْوَرَى وَيَرْوِى لُطْفَهُ كُلُّ نَسِيمٍ سَرَي
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahu qad kamula bi-al-faṣāḥati wa-al-malāḥati wa-tahattakat fī ḥusnihi al-warā wa-yarwī luṭfahu kullu nasīmin sarā
sentences.l: And he-found-him (that he) had become-perfect in the eloquence and the comeliness, and mankind threw-off-all-restraint over his-beauty, and every breeze (that) travelled-by-night relates his-grace.
sentences.i: And he found him grown perfect in eloquence and good looks; all mankind cast off restraint for love of his beauty, and every breeze that stirred by night carried tidings of his grace.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-faṣāḥa / al-malāḥa, then al-warā / sarā. wajada + object + qad + perfect, “found him to have become …”. kamula, “to be complete, perfect”, with bi-, “in (respect of)”. tahattaka, Form V of hataka, “to rend (a veil)”, is “to have one's veil torn, be disgraced”, and so of lovers “to throw off all reserve, be openly infatuated”; fī, “over, on account of”. al-warā, “mankind, all creatures”, is construed as feminine (tahattakat), as collectives often are. yarwī, from rawā, yarwī, “to relate, hand on (a report)”: the night breeze, a messenger between lovers in Arabic poetry, tells of his luṭf, his grace and gentleness. The print has ى (يروى); the active is assumed here, though the passive yurwā luṭfuhu, “his grace is told by”, would mean the same. sarā, “to travel by night”, is an asyndetic relative clause after the indefinite nasīm, “a breeze (that) blew by night”; the print writes it سري, with ي for alif maqṣūra.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ فِتْنَةً فِى الْجَمَالِ لِلْعُشَّاقِ وَرَوْضَةً فِى الْكَمَالِ لِلْمُشْتَاقِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra fitnatan fī al-jamāli li-al-ʿushshāqi wa-rawḍatan fī al-kamāli li-al-mushtāqi
sentences.l: And he-became a-temptation in the beauty for the lovers, and a-garden in the perfection for the longing-one.
sentences.i: In beauty he became a seduction to lovers, and in perfection a garden to every longing heart.
sentences.n: Two balanced members of sajʿ: fitnatan fī al-jamāl li-al-ʿushshāq / rawḍatan fī al-kamāl li-al-mushtāq, rhyming on -āq with jamāl / kamāl chiming inside. ṣāra takes its predicate in the accusative. fitna, “trial, temptation, enchantment”: beauty that leads hearts astray. li-, “for, to”, marks those it affects. ʿushshāq, plural of ʿāshiq, “passionate lover”; mushtāq, Form VIII participle, “one who longs”. Here the print writes fī with ى (فى), though in the sentence before it has في.

sentences.t: عَذْبُ الْكَلَامِ يُخْجِلُ وَجْهُهُ بَدْرَ التَّمَامِ
sentences.tr: ʿadhbu al-kalāmi yukhjilu wajhuhu badra al-tamāmi
sentences.l: Sweet of the speech; his-face puts-to-shame the full-moon of the completeness.
sentences.i: Sweet of speech, he had a face that put the full moon to shame.
sentences.n: Now the description runs on as a chain of epithets with no main verb. ʿadhbu al-kalāmi, “sweet of speech”: an adjective annexed to a noun that names the respect in which it holds (an “improper” iḍāfa). It is pointed as nominative, the predicate of an unexpressed “he (is)”; the print gives no cases, and an accusative carrying on from ṣāra is possible. yukhjilu, Form IV, “to make ashamed”: subject wajhuhu, object badra. badr al-tamām, “the moon of completeness”, the full moon. Rhyme: al-kalām / al-tamām.

sentences.t: صَاحِبُ قَدٍّ وَاعْتِدَالٍ وَظَرْفٍ وَدَلَالٍ كَأَنَّهُ غُصْنُ بَانٍ أَوْ قَضِيبُ خَيْزُرَانٍ
sentences.tr: ṣāḥibu qaddin wa-iʿtidālin wa-ẓarfin wa-dalālin ka-annahu ghuṣnu bānin aw qaḍību khayzurānin
sentences.l: Owner of stature and straightness and grace and coquetry, as-though-he (were) a-bough of ban or a-rod of rattan.
sentences.i: Tall and well made, graceful and full of charm, he was like a branch of the ban tree or a wand of supple cane.
sentences.n: ṣāḥib, “possessor of”, + genitive: “a man of stature …”. qadd, “stature, figure”, and iʿtidāl, Form VIII verbal noun, “being straight and evenly proportioned”: the tall, upright figure is the ideal. The rhyme pairs iʿtidāl / dalāl, then bān / khayzurān. ka-annahu, “as though he (were)”: ka-, “like”, + anna, “that”, with -hu as its subject; the print writes كانه with a bare alif. The bān is the ben tree (Moringa), whose slender, swaying boughs are the stock image of a graceful figure; khayzurān, “rattan, cane”, stands for suppleness.

sentences.t: يَنُوبُ خَدُّهُ عَنِ الْوَرْدِ وَشَقَائِقِ النُّعْمَانِ وَقَدُّهُ عَنْ غُصْنِ الْبَانِ
sentences.tr: yanūbu khadduhu ʿani al-wardi wa-shaqāʾiqi al-nuʿmāni wa-qadduhu ʿan ghuṣni al-bāni
sentences.l: His-cheek stands-in for the rose and the anemones of al-Nuʿmān, and his-stature for the bough of the ban.
sentences.i: His cheek could stand in for the rose and the anemone, and his figure for the bough of the ban tree.
sentences.n: The print has خدة, a misprint for خده, corrected here. The print has وقدة, a misprint for وقده, corrected here. In both the pronoun ه, “his”, has been set as ة. nāba ʿan, “to take the place of, stand in for”: the verb chooses ʿan. The second clause borrows the verb of the first: wa-qadduhu (yanūbu) ʿan …. shaqāʾiq al-nuʿmān is the red anemone; the name is traditionally tied to the Lakhmid king al-Nuʿmān, though some derive it from nuʿmān, “blood”. Rhyme: al-nuʿmān / al-bān. The hamza of شقائق is printed.

sentences.t: ظَرِيفُ الشَّمَائِلِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الْقَائِلُ
sentences.tr: ẓarīfu al-shamāʾili ka-mā qāla fīhi al-qāʾilu
sentences.l: Graceful of the qualities, as said about-him the sayer:
sentences.i: Charming in all his ways, as the poet said of him:
sentences.n: ẓarīf al-shamāʾil, another adjective annexed to its noun, “graceful in his manners”; shamāʾil, plural of shimāl, “natural dispositions, bearing”. ka-mā qāla …, “as … said”: ka-, “like, as”, + mā, the stock formula for bringing in verse. qāla fīhi, “said about him”: fī marks the subject of the verses. al-qāʾil, “the sayer”, the unnamed poet. Rhyme: al-shamāʾil / al-qāʾil. The hamzas of الشمائل and القائل are printed.

sentences.t:
بَدَا فَقَالُوا تَبَارَكَ اللّٰهُ * جَلَّ الَّذِيْ صَاغَهُ وَسَوَّاهُ
مَلِيكُ كُلِّ الْمِلَاحِ قَاطِبَةً * فَكُلُّهُمْ اَصْبَحُوْا رَعَايَاهُ
فِي رِيقِهِ شُهْدَةٌ مُذَوَّبَةٌ * وَانْعَقَدَ الدُّرُّ فِي ثَنَايَاهُ
مُكَمَّلًا بِالْجَمَالِ مُنْفَرِدًا * كُلُّ الْوَرٰى فِي جَمَالِهِ تَاهُوْا
قَدْ كَتَبَ الْحُسْنُ فَوْقَ وَجْنَتِهِ * اَشْهَدُ اَنْ لَا مَلِيحَ اِلَّا هُوْ
sentences.tr:
badā fa-qālū tabāraka Allāhu * jalla alladhī ṣāghahu wa-sawwāhu
malīku kulli al-milāḥi qāṭibatan * fa-kulluhum aṣbaḥū raʿāyāhu
fī rīqihi shuhdatun mudhawwabatun * wa-inʿaqada al-durru fī thanāyāhu
mukammalan bi-al-jamāli munfaridan * kullu al-warā fī jamālihi tāhū
qad kataba al-ḥusnu fawqa wajnatihi * ashhadu an lā malīḥa illā hū
sentences.l:
He-appeared, and they-said: Blessed-is God! * Exalted (is) He-who fashioned-him and shaped-him-evenly.
King of all the comely-ones, altogether: * for all-of-them have-become his-subjects.
In his-saliva (is) a-honeycomb melted, * and the pearl is-knotted (in rows) in his-front-teeth.
Perfected with the beauty, alone-of-his-kind: * all mankind in his-beauty have-strayed.
The beauty has-written over his-cheek: * I-bear-witness that there-is-no comely-one but he.
sentences.i:
He appeared, and they cried, “Blessed be God! Exalted is He who fashioned him and gave him his perfect form!”
He is king of all the fair, every one of them, and all of them have become his subjects.
In his mouth is honey from the comb, melted, and pearls lie strung in the row of his teeth.
Perfect in beauty, without a peer, he has left all mankind lost and wandering in his loveliness.
Beauty has written on his cheek: “I bear witness that there is none fair but he.”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and are given exactly as printed. The metre appears to be munsariḥ; the rhyme is -āhu, with tāhū and hū in the last two lines. tabāraka allāhu, “blessed is God”, the Qurʾānic exclamation at a marvel of creation; ṣāghahu, “fashioned him” as a goldsmith shapes metal; sawwāhu, Form II, “made him even, gave him just proportions”, a Qurʾānic verb of creation. The print marks long vowels with a sukūn (الَّذِيْ, اَصْبَحُوْا) and writes hamza as a bare alif with a vowel (اَصْبَحُوْا, اَشْهَدُ, اِلَّا). malīk, “king, sovereign”, is an intensive form of malik, used in the Qurʾān (54:55); al-milāḥ, plural of malīḥ, “the comely”; qāṭibatan, adverbial accusative, “all together, without exception”. raʿāyā, plural of raʿiyya, “flock; subjects”. rīq, “saliva”: the beloved's mouth tasting of honey or wine is a commonplace of love poetry. shuhda, “a piece of honeycomb”; mudhawwaba, Form II passive participle, “melted”. inʿaqada, Form VII, “to be knotted, strung”, of pearls set in a row; thanāyā, plural of thaniyya, “the front teeth”, the pearls themselves. mukammalan and munfaridan, “perfected”, “unique”, are circumstantial accusatives with no stated verb, hanging on the “he” of the poem. The print writes al-warā with a dagger alif (الْوَرٰى). tāhū, from tāha, yatīhu, “to stray, be lost, be bewildered”. The last line turns the Muslim profession of faith, ashhadu an lā ilāha illā Allāh, “I bear witness that there is no god but God”, into a profession of love, a daring and much-loved conceit: lā of absolute negation takes malīḥa in the accusative without tanwīn, and hū is huwa, “he”, shortened for the rhyme.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَكَامَلَتْ سَنَةٌ أُخْرَى لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ دَعَاهُ وَالِدُهُ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي أَمَا تَسْمَعُ مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā takāmalat sanatun ukhrā li-Qamari al-Zamāni daʿāhu wāliduhu ilayhi wa-qāla lahu yā waladī amā tasmaʿu minnī
sentences.l: And when was-completed another year for Qamar al-Zamān, his-father called-him to-himself and said to-him: O my-son, do-you not hear from-me?
sentences.i: When another full year had come round for Qamar al-Zamān, his father summoned him and said, “My son, will you not listen to me?”
sentences.n: The print has والدة, a misprint for والده, corrected here: wāliduhu, “his father”; with the tāʾ marbūṭa the word would mean “mother”. takāmala, Form VI, “to be completed, come round in full”. li-Qamari al-Zamāni: li- marks whose year it is, i.e. another year of his age. daʿāhu … ilayhi, “called him to himself”, i.e. summoned him. amā, the negative question, expects agreement: “will you not …?” samiʿa min, “to hear from”, here means “to listen to, heed”. The shadda of فلمّا is printed.

sentences.t: فَوَقَعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ بَيْنَ يَدَيْ وَالِدِهِ هَيْبَةً وَاسْتَحَى مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-waqaʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalā al-arḍi bayna yaday wālidihi haybatan wa-istaḥā minhu
sentences.l: And fell Qamar al-Zamān on the-ground between the-two-hands of his-father (out of) awe, and was-abashed before-him.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān threw himself to the ground before his father in awe, abashed in his presence,
sentences.n: The print again has والدة, a misprint for والده, corrected here. bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, means “before, in the presence of”. haybatan, accusative of cause: “out of awe”. istaḥā, the short form of istaḥyā, Form X, “to feel shame, be abashed”; min marks the person before whom one is abashed. Falling to the ground is the prostration owed to a king.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَبَتِ كَيْفَ لَا أَسْمَعُ مِنْكَ وَقَدْ أَمَرَنِي اللَّهُ بِطَاعَتِكَ وَأَنْ لَا أَعْصِيَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā abati kayfa lā asmaʿu minka wa-qad amaranī Allāhu bi-ṭāʿatika wa-an lā aʿṣiyaka
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: O my-father, how (could) I not hear from-you, when has-commanded-me God with obedience-to-you, and that I-not disobey-you?
sentences.i: and said, “Father, how could I not listen to you, when God has commanded me to obey you and never to defy you?”
sentences.n: yā abati, the affectionate vocative “O my father”, with the -ti of address in place of the pronoun -ī. wa-qad + perfect here is circumstantial: “when God has already commanded”. amara bi-, “to command (someone) to”: the verb takes bi- for the thing commanded, ṭāʿatika, “obedience to you” (the suffix names the one obeyed). The command goes on with a clause, wa-an lā aʿṣiyaka, an + subjunctive. Obedience to parents is a duty laid down in the Qurʾān, which the son is echoing.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ يَا وَلَدِي اعْلَمْ أَنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُزَوِّجَكَ وَأَفْرَحَ بِكَ فِي حَيَوٰتِي وَأُسَلْطِنَكَ فِي مَمْلَكَتِي قَبْلَ مَمَاتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku Shahramānu yā waladī iʿlam annī urīdu an uzawwijaka wa-afraḥa bika fī ḥayātī wa-usalṭinaka fī mamlakatī qabla mamātī
sentences.l: So said to-him the-king Shahramān: O my-son, know that-I want that I-marry-you-off and rejoice in-you in my-life (-ātī), and make-you-sultan in my-kingdom before my-death (-ātī).
sentences.i: King Shahramān said to him, “My son, know that I wish to see you married and have joy of you while I live, and to make you sultan over my kingdom before I die.”
sentences.n: an governs three subjunctives in a row: uzawwijaka, afraḥa, usalṭinaka. zawwaja, Form II, “to give in marriage, marry off”. fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice in”: bi- marks the source of the joy. usalṭinaka, from the quadriliteral salṭana, “to make (someone) sultan”, a post-classical verb built on sulṭān. The rhyme falls on ḥayātī / mamātī, “my life / my death”. ḥayātī is spelt in the old Qurʾanic way, حيوة with wāw and a dagger alif; read ḥayātī.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنْ أَبِيهِ ذَلِكَ أَطْرَقَ رَأْسَهُ سَاعَةً ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa min abīhi dhālika aṭraqa raʾsahu sāʿatan thumma rafaʿa raʾsahu
sentences.l: And when he-heard from his-father that, he-lowered his-head an-hour, then raised his-head
sentences.i: When he heard this from his father he bowed his head for a while, then raised it
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, “to lower the eyes, fall silent with bowed head”; Classical uses it alone or with bi-raʾsihi, but here it takes raʾsahu as a direct object, as it often does in the Nights. sāʿatan, accusative of duration: sāʿa is “a while”, not a clock hour. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا أَبَتِ هَذَا شَيْءٌ لَا أَفْعَلُهُ أَبَدًا وَلَوْ سُقِيتُ كَأْسَ الرَّدَى
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā abati hādhā shayʾun lā afʿaluhu abadan wa-law suqītu kaʾsa al-radā
sentences.l: and said: O my-father, this (is) a-thing I-do-not do-it ever, even-if I-were-given-to-drink the-cup of the-perdition.
sentences.i: and said, “Father, this is something I will never do, though I be made to drink the cup of death.
sentences.n: He repeats his refusal from Night 170 almost word for word. lā afʿaluhu abadan: lā + imperfect with abadan looks to the future, “I will never do it”. wa-law, “even if”, with a perfect: suqītu, passive of saqā, “I were given to drink”. al-radā, “ruin, death”. The hamzas of شيء and كأس are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَعْلَمُ يَقِينًا أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى فَرَضَ عَلَيَّ طَاعَتَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā aʿlamu yaqīnan anna Allāha taʿālā faraḍa ʿalayya ṭāʿataka
sentences.l: And I know (for-)certain that God, exalted (is He), has-imposed upon-me obedience-to-you;
sentences.i: I know for certain that God Most High has made obedience to you my duty;
sentences.n: wa-anā aʿlamu, a circumstantial clause, “while I know”: he concedes the point before refusing. yaqīnan, adverbial accusative, “with certainty”. faraḍa ʿalā, “to impose as a duty on”; farḍ is the legal term for a binding obligation. taʿālā, “exalted is He”, the customary praise after the name of God. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَبِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ لَا تُكَلِّفْنِي فِي أَمْرِ الزَّوَاجِ وَلَا تَظُنَّ أَنِّي أَتَزَوَّجُ طُولَ عُمْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-bi-Allāhi ʿalayka lā tukallifnī fī amri al-zawāji wa-lā taẓunna annī atazawwaju ṭūla ʿumrī
sentences.l: so by-God upon-you, do-not burden-me in (the) matter of the-marriage, and do-not think that-I (will) marry the-length of my-life,
sentences.i: so I beg you by God, do not press me in this matter of marriage, and do not think that I will marry as long as I live;
sentences.n: The print has الزاوج, a misprint for الزواج, corrected here; the word is printed correctly a few lines earlier. bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, a formula of earnest entreaty. lā tukallifnī: prohibitive lā with the jussive of kallafa, Form II, “to lay a burden on, press (someone) to do”; Classical puts the task in the accusative, here it comes with fī, “in the matter of”. lā taẓunna: jussive of the doubled verb ẓanna, which keeps its doubling with a helping -a. ṭūla ʿumrī, accusative of time, “the length of my life”, i.e. ever.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّنِي قَرَأْتُ كُتُبًا لِلْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ وَالْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ وَاطَّلَعْتُ عَلَى مَا وَقَعَ لَهُمْ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ مِنَ الْفِتَنِ وَالْآفَاتِ وَمَكْرِهِنَّ غَيْرِ الْمُتَنَاهِي وَمَا يَحْدُثُ عَنْهُنَّ مِنَ الدَّوَاهِي
sentences.tr: li-annanī qaraʾtu kutuban li-al-mutaqaddimīna wa-al-mutaʾakhkhirīna wa-iṭṭalaʿtu ʿalā mā waqaʿa lahum mina al-nisāʾi mina al-fitani wa-al-āfāti wa-makrihinna ghayri al-mutanāhī wa-mā yaḥduthu ʿanhunna mina al-dawāhī
sentences.l: because-I have-read books of the-former-ones and the-latter-ones, and acquainted-myself with what befell them from the-women of the-trials and the-blights, and their-cunning, the-not-ending (-āhī), and what arises from-them of the-calamities (-āhī).
sentences.i: for I have read the books of the ancients and the moderns, and learned what trials and afflictions befell them at the hands of women, and of women's boundless guile, and of the calamities that spring from them.
sentences.n: li-annanī, “because I”: li- + anna, with the fuller suffix -nī. li-al-mutaqaddimīna wa-al-mutaʾakhkhirīna: li- marks the authors, “books by the earlier and the later (writers)”, a stock pair for every authority, old and new. iṭṭalaʿa, Form VIII, “to look into, become acquainted with”, takes ʿalā for what one learns of. The first min (mina al-nisāʾi) marks the source, “from women”; the second (mina al-fitani) spells out the mā, “what … in the way of trials and blights”. makrihinna is genitive, most naturally a second object of ʿalā beside mā (as is the following wa-mā yaḥduthu), though it could also hang on the min of al-fitani; ghayri al-mutanāhī agrees with it: “their unending cunning”. The rhyme falls on al-mutanāhī / al-dawāhī. The shaddas of للمتقدّمين and واطّلعت, the hamza of والمتأخرين and the madda of الآفات are printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aḥsana qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And how fine (is) the-saying of the-poet!
sentences.i: How well the poet has put it:
sentences.n: mā aḥsana …, the verb of wonder: mā + afʿala, with its object in the accusative, “how fine is the saying of …!” The formula introduces verse throughout the Nights.

sentences.t:
مَنْ كَادَهُ الْعَاهِرَاتُ * فَلَا يَرَى مِنْ خَلَاصِ
وَلَوْ بَنَى اَلْفَ حِصْنٍ * مُشَيَّدَةً بِالرَّصَاصِ
فَلَيْسَ يُجْدِي بِنَاهَا * وَلَا تُفِيْدُ الصَّيَاصِي
اِنَّ النِّسَاءَ خَائِنَاتٌ * لِكُلِّ دَانٍ وَقَاصِ
مُخَضَّبَاتُ بَنَانٍ * مُظَفَّرَاتُ عِقَاصِ
مُكَحَّلَاتُ جُفُونٍ * مُجَرَّعَاتُ غِصَاصِ
sentences.tr:
man kādahu al-ʿāhirātu * fa-lā yarā min khalāṣi
wa-law banā alfa ḥiṣnin * mushayyadatan bi-al-raṣāṣi
fa-laysa yujdī bināhā * wa-lā tufīdu al-ṣayāṣī
inna al-nisāʾa khāʾinātun * li-kulli dānin wa-qāṣi
mukhaḍḍabātu banānin * muẓaffarātu ʿiqāṣi
mukaḥḥalātu jufūnin * mujarraʿātu ghiṣāṣi
sentences.l:
Whoever the-harlots plot-against-him, * he-does-not see (any) of deliverance (-āṣī),
even-if he-built a-thousand fortresses * built-high with the-lead (-āṣī);
for not avails their-building, * nor profit the-strongholds (-āṣī).
Indeed the-women (are) betrayers * to every near-one and far-one (-āṣī),
henna-dyed of fingertip, * braided of locks (-āṣī),
kohl-lined of eyelids, * made-to-gulp of chokings (-āṣī).
sentences.i:
He whom harlots plot to snare will find no way out,
though he build a thousand forts made fast with lead;
their walls will not avail him, nor their towers serve.
Women are false to every man, the near and the far,
their fingertips red with henna, their tresses braided,
their eyelids lined with kohl, and choking draughts their portion.
sentences.n: The print points this poem fully, and it is copied as printed. The rhyme is -āṣī, and the words bend to it: khalāṣi and qāṣi (for qāṣin, “far”) drop their tanwīn at the rhyme, and bināhā is bināʾuhā, “their building”, with the hamza dropped. kādahu, “plotted against him”: the -hu takes up man, “whoever”. alf has a hamza of its own (the print marks its alif with a fatḥa), so it is not elided after banā. mushayyadatan, “raised high and strong”, is feminine because it treats the thousand forts as a non-human plural; walls sealed with molten lead are the proverbial last word in strength. yujdī, “avails”; al-ṣayāṣī, “strongholds” (sg. ṣīṣiya), a Qurʾanic word. The sukūn on the long ī of تُفِيْدُ is a habit of the print's verse pointing. dānin wa-qāṣin, “near and far”, means everyone. The last two lines are strings of Form II participles in an “improper” iḍāfa, the indefinite genitive saying in what respect: mukhaḍḍabātu banānin, “henna-dyed as to fingertips”. muẓaffarāt, “braided”, is printed with ẓ for the expected ḍ (muḍaffarāt, from ḍafara, “to plait”), a common confusion of the two letters; ʿiqāṣ, “plaited locks” (sg. ʿaqīṣa). The last phrase is doubtful. jarraʿa is “to make (someone) gulp down”, and the passive pointing mujarraʿātu gives “made to gulp chokings”; the sense rather wants the active mujarriʿātu, “who make (men) gulp choking draughts”. ghiṣāṣ looks like a plural of ghuṣṣa, “a lump in the throat, a choking grief”, perhaps made for the rhyme. The print's reading is kept.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aḥsana qawla al-ākhari
sentences.l: And how fine (is) the-saying of the-other!
sentences.i: And how well another has put it:
sentences.n: al-ākhar, “the other”, here “another poet”. The madda of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t:
اِنَّ النِّسَاءَ وَاِنْ دُعِينَ لِعِفَّةٍ * رِمَمٌ تُقَلِّبُهَا النُّسُورُ الْحُوَّمُ
فِى اللَّيْلِ عِنْدَكَ سِرُّهَا وَحَدِيثُهَا * وَغَدٍ لِغَيْرِكَ سَاقُهَا وَالْمِعْصَمُ
كَالْخَانِ تُسْكِنُهُ وَتُصْبِحُ رَاحِلاً * فَيَحُلُّ بَعْدَكَ فِيهِ مَنْ لَا تَعْلَمُ
sentences.tr:
inna al-nisāʾa wa-in duʿīna li-ʿiffatin * rimamun tuqallibuhā al-nusūru al-ḥuwwamu
fī al-layli ʿindaka sirruhā wa-ḥadīthuhā * wa-ghadin li-ghayrika sāquhā wa-al-miʿṣamu
ka-al-khāni tuskinuhu wa-tuṣbiḥu rāḥilan * fa-yaḥullu baʿdaka fīhi man lā taʿlamu
sentences.l:
Indeed the-women, even-if they-are-called to-chastity, * (are) carrion, turn-it-over the-vultures, the-circling-ones (-amu).
In the-night with-you (are) her-secret and her-talk, * and tomorrow for-other-than-you (are) her-shank and the-wrist (-amu).
(She is) like the-inn: you-lodge-in-it, and you-become-at-morning departing, * then alights after-you in-it whom you-do-not know (-amu).
sentences.i:
Women, though they be called to chastity, are carrion turned over by the wheeling vultures.
By night her secrets and her talk are yours; tomorrow her leg and her wrist are another's.
She is an inn: you lodge in it and at dawn ride on, and after you a stranger comes to stay.
sentences.n: Kāmil metre, fully pointed in the print and copied as printed; the rhyme is -amu. duʿīna, passive of daʿā, feminine plural, “they are called”; li- marks what they are called to. rimam, plural of rimma, “rotting bones, carrion”; al-ḥuwwam, plural of ḥāʾim, of birds wheeling round and round. From the second line the women become a singular “she”: -hā is each one of them. wa-ghadin, “and tomorrow”, stands in the genitive, as if still governed by the fī of fī al-layli; one would expect the adverbial accusative ghadan. sāq is the leg from knee to ankle, miʿṣam the wrist where the bracelet sits. ka-al-khāni: ka-, “like”, governs the genitive. tuskinuhu is pointed as Form IV, which properly means “to make (someone) dwell”; the sense wants “you lodge in it”, Classical taskunuhu (Form I), so the print's vowels may be mistaken; they are kept. In scansion the pronoun is lengthened, tuskinuhū. aṣbaḥa, “to be at morning”, takes its predicate in the accusative: rāḥilan, “departing”. ḥalla fī, “to alight in, put up at”. The print writes فِى with ى, as it often does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ مِنْ وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَفَهِمَ الشِّعْرَ وَالنِّظَامَ لَمْ يَرُدَّ عَلَيْهِ جَوَابًا مِنْ فَرْطِ مَحَبَّتِهِ لَهُ وَزَادَهُ مِنْ إِنْعَامِهِ وَإِكْرَامِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Shahramānu min waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni hādhā al-kalāma wa-fahima al-shiʿra wa-al-niẓāma lam yarudda ʿalayhi jawāban min farṭi maḥabbatihi lahu wa-zādahu min inʿāmihi wa-ikrāmihi
sentences.l: And when heard the-king Shahramān from his-son Qamar al-Zamān this speech (-ām), and understood the-poetry and the-arrangement (-ām), he-did-not return to-him an-answer, from excess of his-love for-him, and he-increased-him from his-favouring (-āmihi) and his-honouring (-āmihi).
sentences.i: When King Shahramān heard these words from his son Qamar al-Zamān and took in the verses and their art, he gave him no answer, so great was his love for him, and he heaped yet more favour and honour upon him.
sentences.n: Two rhymes: al-kalāma / al-niẓāma and inʿāmihi / ikrāmihi. al-shiʿr wa-al-niẓām, “the poetry and the composition”: niẓām, literally the stringing of pearls, is the craft of verse. lam yarudda ʿalayhi jawāban, “he returned him no answer”: lam + jussive, the doubled verb keeping its doubling with a helping -a; ʿalā marks the one answered. The shadda of يردّ is printed. min farṭi, “out of the excess of”: min of cause. zādahu min, “gave him more of”: min is partitive. inʿām, verbal noun of anʿama (Form IV), “bestowing favour”; ikrām, of akrama, “showing honour”.

sentences.t: وَانْفَضَّ ذَلِكَ الْمَجْلِسُ مِنْ تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-infaḍḍa dhālika al-majlisu min tilka al-sāʿati
sentences.l: And broke-up that sitting from that hour.
sentences.i: And the audience broke up there and then.
sentences.n: infaḍḍa, Form VII of faḍḍa, “to break up, disperse”, of a gathering. majlis, a place of sitting, hence the session or audience held there. min tilka al-sāʿati, “from that hour”, i.e. at once.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ انْفِضَاضِ الْمَجْلِسِ دَعَا الْمَلِكُ بِوَزِيرِهِ وَاخْتَلَي بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda infiḍāḍi al-majlisi daʿā al-maliku bi-wazīrihi wa-ikhtalā bihi
sentences.l: And after the-breaking-up of the-sitting, called the-king for his-vizier and was-alone with-him,
sentences.i: When the audience had dispersed, the king sent for his vizier and took him aside,
sentences.n: infiḍāḍ, verbal noun of infaḍḍa, just used. daʿā bi-, “to call for, send for”: with bi- the person is fetched, not merely addressed. ikhtalā bi-, Form VIII of khalā, “to be alone with”: bi- marks the companion. The print spells it اختلي, with yāʾ for the final alif maqṣūra, a habit of the text; read ikhtalā.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَخْبِرْنِي مَا الَّذِي أَفْعَلُهُ فِي وَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ قَضِيَّةِ الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-wazīru akhbirnī mā alladhī afʿaluhu fī waladī Qamari al-Zamāni min qaḍiyyati al-zawāji
sentences.l: and said to-him: O the-vizier, inform-me, what (is) that-which I-do in my-son Qamar al-Zamān from (the) case of the-marriage?
sentences.i: and said to him, “Vizier, tell me, what am I to do with my son Qamar al-Zamān in this matter of marriage?”
sentences.n: ayyuhā introduces a vocative noun with the article: “O vizier”. mā alladhī afʿaluhu, “what is it that I am to do”: the imperfect carries “should”. faʿala fī, “to deal with”, fī marking the person dealt with. min qaḍiyyati al-zawāji, “in the matter of marriage”: min is “as regards”; qaḍiyya is a case or affair.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And overtook Shahrazād the-morning (-āḥ), and she-fell-silent from the-speech the-permitted (-āḥ).
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, rhyming al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi. The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning. The print sets the name as one word here.
